item.title: Are You Missing Out in Life Because of Fear?
item.description:
Fear

Are You Missing Out in Life Because of Fear?

Sometimes fear isn't easily recognized but controls the decisions you make.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • There's a difference between preferring not to do something and being fearful of doing it.
  • Feeling uncomfortable may really be fear.
  • Avoidance feeds anxiety so the more you avoid, the more anxious you are likely to become.
Source: AI-Generated

Fear has a purpose. Though uncomfortable, fear protects you by warning you when you're in danger. But fear doesn’t necessarily check to see whether the risk is real before it screams “Danger!” It can show up when there's no reason to experience fear. And you know what? It can show up in ways you may not recognize as being fear. It can be sneaky.

Sometimes fear shows up as discomfort. "I'm not comfortable" can be true, and it can also be an excuse to avoid something. If you respond to fear by avoiding whatever caused it, you can wind up avoiding more and more. Fear starts making decisions for you and it's often not a very good decision-maker. How often do you perhaps label fear as discomfort, and avoid doing activities or interacting with people?

What Being Controlled By Fear Looks Like in Everyday Life

Many people aren't even aware that some of their decisions are fear-based. Consider these situations. Do they sound like you?

The events you don’t show up for

A friend invites you to a party. You want to go, or at least part of you does. You’ve turned down the last few invitations and your friend seems to be getting annoyed that you never show up.

The day comes and you don’t go. You thought of all kinds of reasons why staying home made sense. You feel relieved but also feel guilt and disappointment for letting your friend down, again.

The conversation you rehearse but never have

You want to introduce yourself to someone new, speak up in a meeting, or invite a friend to lunch. You practice in your head first, looking for a way that you wouldn’t feel like a loser afterward. But you can’t be sure how you’ll come across, so you keep quiet. It’s a missed opportunity. You may even build up some resentment about being overlooked without realizing that you’re not taking the opportunities you have to be seen.

The hobby you researched but never started

You looked up dance lessons, cooking lessons, or a local book club. Maybe you marked a cooking class on your calendar. You might even have paid for it, but then you don’t go.

The thought of being a beginner in front of other people is just too much. You know logically that everyone has to start somewhere, but that doesn’t make you want to walk through the door. And that idea of making those quesadillas for your family gets squashed.

The trips you think about, maybe plan, but don't take

You’ve wanted to travel for years, but somehow it’s never the right time.

There are plenty of reasons. Planning feels overwhelming. You wouldn’t know anyone there. You might get lost. What if something goes wrong at home while you’re gone? So you tell yourself you’ll do it someday. If you’ve been saying that for years, fear may have more to do with it than you might think.

The relationship that stays surface-level

You have people in your life you like but don’t feel close to. Getting closer would require being a little more open, and that feels risky in a way that’s sometimes hard to explain.

Maybe you don’t want to be judged. Or you don’t want someone to know how much you care about the friendship. You might not know what you’re afraid of, you just know that opening up is uncomfortable, so you don’t do much of it. The relationship stays comfortable but distant, and you stay lonely.

The job, project, or creative work you never pursued

You’ve thought about doing something that would require putting yourself out there like applying for a promotion, starting a project, or writing a book. Whatever it is, there’s a chance you could fail. Fear of failure stops you.

The medical appointment you’ve been putting off

You know you should go to the doctor, but something about it keeps getting in the way. Maybe it’s the uncertainty of what they might find. Maybe it’s the loss of control that comes with being a patient, or the discomfort in waiting for test results. So you put it off until the worry about not going finally becomes worse than the worry about going. Sometimes people wait long enough that something that would have been relatively easy to take care of becomes much more complicated.

The difficult conversation you’ve been avoiding

There’s a conversation you need to have with a partner, friend, family member, or coworker. You’ve thought about what to say many times. But you don’t know what the other person will say. They could get angry or hurt. You keep waiting for the right moment. In the meantime, there’s tension and maybe resentment because the issue isn’t being addressed. Maybe you get kind of snippy, and your emotions come out sideways.

What Is Your Fear Actually Protecting You From?

Think about the examples above and examples in your own life. What is the actual danger in most of them? Often there isn’t any. You may be protecting yourself from feeling awkward, rejected, or not knowing what to say. Those experiences can be uncomfortable, but they aren’t dangerous.

Here's the takeaway. Even though you may feel better in the short run, what we know for sure is that avoidance maintains anxiety (Barlow, 2002). When you avoid, you don’t have a chance to find out what would have happened if you had stayed or to learn that discomfort is just discomfort. Maybe the party would have been awkward for the first 20 minutes and then fun. Maybe you would have stumbled over your words in the meeting and nobody would have cared.

Preference or Fear: How Do You Know?

This doesn’t mean that every time you say no, you’re avoiding. Sometimes you don’t want to go to the party. I turn down things I don’t want to do and I’m guessing you do too.So how do you tell the difference?

Look at the pattern rather than one decision.

  • Do you keep saying you want to travel but never go anywhere?
  • Do you want friends but turn down invitations?
  • Do you want to move ahead at work but stay quiet when there are opportunities to be noticed?
  • Have you been talking about taking that class for a while now?

Another clue is how you feel afterward. There’s a difference between being glad you chose not to do something and being relieved that you escaped doing it. If you are feeling relief, then there's probably fear involved.

You can also ask yourself, “If I weren’t afraid, would I want to do this?” If the answer is no, fine. Maybe you simply don’t want to do it. If the answer is yes, then fear may be making a decision that you’d rather make for yourself.

Take a look at something you’ve wanted to do and haven’t done.What’s stopping you? If the answer is fear, then the next question is whether you want to keep letting fear make that choice.

item.title: A Tale of Two Hobbies
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

A Tale of Two Hobbies

Personal Perspective: How other people shape our leisure preferences.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Even very different kinds of hobbies have deep commonalities.
  • Social exposure, social influences, and social identities all shape our individual experience of pleasure.
  • These social determinants are often overlooked or forgotten.

How many hobbies have you had? Before you count them, try this definition from an earlier post:

A hobby is a regular, leisure activity that provides meaning and enjoyment to a participant, without any expectation of financial reward.

Though pleasurable by definition, other people’s hobbies can appear boring, weird, or pointless. Want to try competitive worm-charming, or extreme couponing? Perhaps dirt polishing or airline vomit bag collecting is more to your liking. Whatever interests you, your people are out there—in more ways than one!

What’s pleasurable, of course, are the emotional, intellectual, physical, or social rewards stemming from the activity. Less obvious is how we land on certain hobbies instead of others; how we transition from ignorance and indifference to passionate involvement; and how we attach value and special meaning to things and ideas we never cared about before.

I’ll offer some directions for addressing these points, looking outward to the hobbyists’ social environment rather than inward to their minds. But first, I describe two of my own potentially boring, weird, and pointless hobbies.

Playing Guitar

I was a young child in 1964 when my cousins spun their new Meet the Beatles record for me. I was smitten. When my family got a record player, that was among the first albums we owned. I played it ceaselessly, and my parents grew to hate it. That made me love it even more.

I wanted to be a Beatle. I begged Mom and Dad for a guitar for more than a year. They finally relented with a starter instrument and weekly lessons. I trained, got pretty good, and gradually saw myself as a guitarist-musician, even if too late to join the Fab Four.

Sustaining my hobby was easy. Brick-and-mortar stores and online vendors offer guitars, accessories, lessons, and music transcripts. I used to play weekend gigs in bands, and I broadcast free concerts from home during the pandemic. But I no longer play out or display symptoms of guitarist’s gear acquisition syndrome.

Coffee Roasting

Instead of buying coffee in stores, I mail-order five-pound bags of “green” coffee beans and roast a few half-pound batches every couple of weeks in a friend’s garage. This may not be as slick and relatable a hobby as the guitar, but it’s rewarding in its own ways.

I brew coffee for the aroma, flavor, and preparation ritual. The roasting process is also soothingly routine: Measure the beans, fill the roaster's hopper, set the time and temperature, listen to the hypnotic whirs and clicks as it does its thing. I read, write, or chat with my friend through the 25-minute cycles.

Coffee’s ardent subculture hosts conferences and discussion boards, and posts instructional videos and reviews. Online stores post massive amounts of information and sell a stunning variety of roasters, brewing equipment, and raw beans.

I’m not a coffee-cultist, only adjacent. (Of course, nobody in a cult thinks they’re in one.) Early on, I pored over “cupping” reviews, learned how to make perfect espresso, and regularly deliberated over equipment purchases. I experimented with vendors, bean varieties, roast times, and temperatures. I posted questions online and learned from mistakes.

Now I order whatever beans distributors have on sale, and they always yield tasty results. I’m not persnickety, probably because I grew up in the Boston area and “ran on Dunkin’.”

Commonalities

Guitar playing and coffee roasting are very different. But as exemplars of hobbies, they share some key elements. Think about your hobbies, and you’ll probably see them, too. We’ll delve deeper in future posts, but here’s where I sneak in a little stealth-theorizing around a few basic concepts.

Exposure. We’re not as original as we may think. I wanted to emulate the oozing cool of the Beatles’ three guitarists. My older brother took music lessons, so I knew those were a thing. Wanting to play guitar and begging parents for the instrument and lessons was hardly an intellectual leap.

I worked at a friend’s coffee shop for a month before my grad school program began. I learned that all store-bought coffee is a crapshoot, and that instant coffee is just crap. I also learned how coffee grows, gets picked, dried, shipped, roasted, and delivered. Years later, I stumbled on the idea that maybe I could roast my own. Soon I was having fun doing it.

Social Influence. My cousins introduced me to the Beatles, and the Beatles cemented my association between guitar-playing and being liked. My parents supplied my first instrument and lessons, while others—mostly musical peers—encouraged my dabblings and shaped my preferences in songs, guitars, and equipment.

My coffee roasting also has social causes and consequences. I learned a lot from folks who created informative websites about their explorations. I rarely complete a roast without interaction, either with my friend whose garage I use, or her grown son when he’s around, or through emails I read and write while the roaster drum turns. I’ve also been encouraged by positive feedback from friends who brew their coffee with my beans.

Social Identity. As my relationship with the guitar grew, other people began referring to me as a “guitarist” or “musician.” I found it flattering and emboldening, and eventually accepted these identities so generously conferred on me.

Self-identifying as a “coffee roaster” traversed a less social path, but social nonetheless. I don’t know any other home roasters, and I didn’t hold public YouTube coffee roastings during the pandemic. But I respond—maybe a little too enthusiastically—to anyone interested enough to ask me a question about the process.

My views on both hobbies have evolved over the years. Where I live in the South, you can’t “swing a cat” (as they say) without hitting other musicians. That tends to sap the specialness right out of that identity. But, ironically, much later in life, I think coffee roasting has become my “cooler” hobby.

item.title: 9 Things the Emotionally Attuned Parent Says to Their Child
item.description:
Child Development

9 Things the Emotionally Attuned Parent Says to Their Child

Nine small shifts in what you say can stop emotional neglect from passing down.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • A child's behavior is driven by their emotions, so helping them manage feelings comes first.
  • Small shifts in how you answer your child's feelings can keep emotional neglect from passing down.
  • You don't have to parent perfectly, only well enough, to raise an emotionally healthy child.
Source: BalanceFormCreative/StockAdobe

As we all swim together through the murky sea of parenting, I offer you some clear answers: three goals to keep in mind at all times, and exactly how to achieve them.

If you've made many parenting mistakes, rest assured: you are not alone.

Let's face it: parenting is hard. For most of us, doing it right means facing our own demons. Because no one is exposed to our flaws, blind spots, or unresolved issues as much as the children who depend on us. As a psychologist who has specialized in childhood emotional neglect for decades, I have seen how easily this happens.

Unfortunately, all those unresolved problems often transfer automatically from ourselves to our children, unless we make a conscious effort to stop them. This is made more or less difficult for us parents by our own childhoods.

The Subtle but Dramatic Impact of Childhood Emotional Neglect

If you grew up with parents who subtly discouraged or discounted your feelings (childhood emotional neglect), for example, then you'll have a natural inclination, outside of your awareness, to do the same with your children. This is why emotional neglect is so rampant in today's world. It transfers, unchecked and unnoticed, from one generation to the next.

This natural transfer process is aided by one simple fact: in today's world, we are all focused primarily on how our children behave. We don't want them to get in trouble at school or irritate others, right?

Although it's very reasonable to assume that teaching a child to behave takes care of the emotional part, nothing could be further from the truth. In reality, it all happens in reverse. Our children's behavior is driven by their emotions. So the best way to help our children behave is to teach them how to manage their feelings.

The Keys to Emotional Intelligence

There's another key reason to focus more on emotions with our children. In the last 10 years, a large body of research has found that kids who are good at recognizing, tolerating, expressing, and managing emotions in themselves and others (high emotional intelligence) are more successful academically, make better leaders, and enjoy greater career success as adults.

I know what you're thinking: "OK, so it's important. How do you do it? Behavior is at least concrete and visible, but feelings are hidden, messy, and confusing. What's a parent to do?"

So let's get down to brass tacks. Here are three goals to keep in mind at all times, and exactly how to achieve them.

The 3 Goals of the Emotionally Attuned Parent

  • Your child feels a part of something. They know they’re not alone. You're always on their team.
  • Your child knows that whatever they feel, it's OK, and it matters to you. They will be held accountable for their behavior, but not for their emotions.
  • Your child learns how to tolerate, manage, and express their feelings.

Any parent who accomplishes these skills well enough is raising an emotionally healthy child and an emotionally intelligent child. You don't have to do it perfectly. You just have to do it well enough.

What to Say Instead

  1. Instead of "Stop crying," say, "Why are you crying?"
  2. Instead of "Let me know when you're done with your fit," say, "That's OK. Get it all out. Then we'll talk."
  3. Instead of "Alright, enough! I'm done with this," say, "Let's take a break so we can both calm down."
  4. Instead of "Fix the attitude!" say, "You sound angry or upset. Are you?"
  5. Instead of "You need to think before you act!" say, "How'd this go wrong? Let's think it through."
  6. Instead of "Go to your room until you can behave better," say, "I see you're angry. Is it because…?"
  7. Instead of "OK, OK, stop crying now so we can go in the store," say, "Look at me. Take a deep breath. Let's count to five."
  8. Instead of "There's nothing to be nervous about," say, "Everyone gets nervous. It's OK. Let's talk."
  9. Instead of "Don't talk to me with that tone," say, "Try saying that again, but nicer so I can hear it."

All children have very intense emotions, but they do not have the skills to manage them. When we are frustrated or overwhelmed by their expression of feeling, it becomes very difficult for us parents to manage what we're feeling so that we can respond the right way to what they're feeling.

No one sets out purposely to shame their child for having emotions. But the way we respond can easily, in very subtle ways, communicate to a child that they shouldn't be feeling what they're feeling.

Keep in mind that virtually all children have heard everything in the first column many times, and it's OK. It will only cause harm (childhood emotional neglect) if the child receives the subtle, unstated messages below too frequently:

  • Your feelings are excessive.
  • Your feeling is wrong.
  • I don't want to know what you're feeling.
  • Your feelings are an inconvenience for me.
  • You need to deal with this alone.
  • I don't care what you feel; I only care about your behavior.

It's Never Too Late to Respond Differently

If you winced a bit while you read those messages above, don't despair! It's not your fault. You're simply doing what human beings do, and responding to your children as you were responded to as a child. Rest assured, it is never too late to start responding differently.

Try using the emotionally attuned responses above as regularly as possible, keeping in mind that you will never be perfect, because no one is. Watch and see if, over time, your child starts to respond to you differently. Watch to see how their behavior changes as they learn how to manage their own feelings.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com.

item.title: 7 Tools to Help You Maintain a Positive Attitude
item.description:
Optimism

7 Tools to Help You Maintain a Positive Attitude

Having a positive attitude: We tend to find what we look for in life.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • When you look for good things, you tend to find them. This reinforces optimism.
  • When you tend to observe the negatives in your life, you can develop a self-defeating life perspective.
  • When you think in a positive way, your mind works hard to put your intentions into play.
Source: Marek Uliasz/Shutterstock

The first lesson I teach most of my patients is how to frame things in a positive way, by thinking about what they do want rather than what they do not want.

When people look for good things, they tend to find them, and this reinforces an optimistic belief that life is good. Conversely, when they think about what they do not want, they tend to observe the negative in their lives, which can lead them to develop a self-defeating life perspective.

I teach several tools that help maintain a positive attitude, as described in my book, The Life Guide for Teens:

Words in Many Forms

In order to make the positive words you choose “stick,” use them in more ways than one. Writing them, saying them aloud, singing them, or incorporating them in artwork all create more activity in your brain than just reading them.

For example, a great way is to write USE POSITIVE WORDS on a notecard, decorate it with positive images, and tape it on your mirror or your nightstand. The more you see, read, and say the words, the more attention your subconscious will pay to them—and the more it’ll help you follow through.

Focus on Your Effort

One of the things every person learns is that you can’t always control what happens, but you can usually control what you think and do. That’s why I AM, I WILL, I CAN, and I DID are powerful phrases to incorporate into your everyday vocabulary.

Focusing on what you do is a way of declaring you have the power to make things happen. So, whatever you're doing, own it and say it out loud. This will get both the conscious and subconscious parts of your mind engaged in helping you.

Be Careful With “NOT”

Like someone who’s eavesdropping from across the room, your brain tends to focus on the main words in your statements. Be wise and choosy about those.

For example, consider the sentence, “I will not cheat on the test.”

Which word jumps out at you?

I’ll bet it’s cheat. That’s the action. It’s the problem. And thinking about it is unhelpful as it might even cause you to be more tempted to cheat.

Instead, you could simply say, “I’ll be honest and do my best work on the test.” This gets the brain thinking about how to do well in a truthful way.

“Not” is a tricky word for your subconscious to deal with. It’s rarely the main word in a sentence—not the main subject and not the important action. Because of that, make statements that say what you will do or what you do want, rather than statements about things you don’t want.

Borrow a Helpful Voice

When you’re struggling to find the right words to deal with a problem, it’s okay to use someone else’s words to help you. Think about someone whose voice you respect and trust—maybe a teacher, a coach, a grandparent, or an older sibling.

What would that person say? You may surprise yourself with how much of their manner and knowledge you’ve made your own. Or think about a famous person who could coach you—maybe Brandi Chastain, The Rock, or Taylor Swift.

If you can’t think of a real-life person in the moment, consider a fictional character. What words might Gandalf use to give you advice? Or Barbie? Or Uncle Iroh? Or Yoda?

Be Specific

Once you begin to use positive words, your conscious and subconscious will work hard to put your intentions into play. You can help both parts of your mind get started by giving them more details about how to accomplish your desires.

For instance, instead of saying “I want to do well on my test tomorrow,” you might say, “I want to do well on my test by being calm, confident, and focused. I want to be able to easily recall what I have learned.” See the difference? The second statement gives you a goal and a way to achieve it.

Block Negative Words

Your brain processes what you hear to decide what to do next. As part of this processing, the conscious and subconscious parts of your mind choose what messages they want to remember after hearing them from the outside world. When you hear positive words, these can help you feel happier or stronger. When you hear negative words, they can cause you to feel sad or weak.

You can block the effect of negative words by countering them in your mind with positive words. For instance, if someone says you are stupid, you can tell yourself that you are smart. If you don’t quite believe you are smart, you can tell yourself that you want and have the power to become smarter, which also blocks the effect of negative words.

Remember: Only you are in charge of how you feel. No one can make you feel bad without your permission.

Help Others

When you understand how powerfully words can affect the mind, you can use them to help people you care about become smarter, stronger, and happier, too.

Use encouraging and positive words with your family members, friends, and teammates. Positive words are even helpful to use with authority figures such as teachers and bosses, because people are more likely to be kind to you if you are kind to them first.

Point to Ponder

Cultivating an optimistic belief that good things will happen in our lives may help us create longer and healthier lives for ourselves.

Research has shown that in comparison to others, optimistic people experience an increase in their life span of up to 15% (Lee et al., 2019). Optimism also is associated with a decrease in our odds of developing dementia by 15% (Stenlund et al., 2026).
